rv.q: The Iowa featured in the new musical 'The Bridges of Madison County' is flat indeed but, oh boy, the voices soar. Kelli O'Hara and Steven Pasquale come just short of blowing the roof off the Theatre in this touching doomed romance that features a superb, thrilling score by Jason Robert Brown.

But although Kelli O’Hara and Steven Pasquale are in glorious voice as this passionate pair, the bombastic orchestrations and Bartlett Sher’s overstated helming inflate the production into some quasi-operatic beast that thinks it’s “Aida.”
The Bridges of Madison County is a musical that knows exactly what it wants to be: a gorgeous, grown-up love story that doesn't apologize for its sentimentality.
Still, when you have a central performance as sensitive, probing and operatically rich and lustrous as Ms. O’Hara’s, you won’t find me kvetching too loudly.
Their story never quite breaks free of the romance genre, but on the other hand, it’s a far sexier telling of “Bridges” than was illuminated in the 1995 movie.
But Kelli O'Hara and Steven Pasquale, magnificently magnetic as Francesca and Robert, make the ripping feel like real heartbreak.
If there is an affair to remember here, it’s the enduring one between O’Hara and the audience.

Fussy direction and design choices and cumbersome book scenes crowd the central couple, but the gorgeous voices and thoughtful characterizations of Kelli O’Hara and Steven Pasquale in those roles help counter the weaknesses of this problematic romantic musical.
Wisely, composer/lyricist Jason Robert Brown, book writer Marsha Norman and director Bartlett Sher attempt to mitigate the book's high-flown verbiage and fantastical air.
The Bridges of Madison County is a perfectly decent musical that feels oddly beside the point.
It's richly melodic and rhythmic — and one of Broadway's best in the last decade.
Mission, I would definitely say, accomplished.
The Bridges of Madison County is a show that knows exactly what it wants to be and achieves it with remarkable consistency and skill.
Ultimately, this is a chamber musical that is both introspective and modest at its core.
It’s so delightful to get caught up in her dilemma.
You enjoy the wonderful performances and the numerous soaring ballads, frustrated that this exceptional work isn't contained in a more workable musical.
Yet there are glimmers of emotional resonance and beauty in Bridges.

As devised by its creators, this slow, static and quiet adaptation of Robert James Waller's bestselling romance novel, which was previously adapted into a hit film with no less than Meryl Streep and Clint Eastwood, is a snooze and a misfire.
She, O’Hara, and Brown make this a Bridge worth crossing, but there’s a toll of excess sentiment you’ll have to pay.
How discouraging that the rest of the enterprise dulls what might have been glorious.
Too bad it couldn't be just that simple an evening.
